transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-02 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~55m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jon (Redwood SE), Nina (CSM), Evan (HarborGuard SRE), Priya (Head of Platform), Liam (Security)

Summary (auto): brief run through of the incident that took place last week; focus on KV eviction cascade + how fallback routing behaved under pressure. Action items captured at the end.

[00:00] Maya Thompson: ok everyone, thanks for making time. I know you all had a rough week, so we want to walk through what we saw and then propose mitigations. Evan, do you want to start with your quick recap?

[00:22] Evan Morales: yeah, sure. thanks. so on tuesday at 02:14 UTC we saw a throughput spike, roughly 3x baseline, a bunch of long tail requests, and shortly after that we observed a series of kv cache evictions across the cluster. throughput was fine but latency jumped and a backpressure loop started. some requests hit fallback routes but the fallback capacity was smaller and caused queued tokens, and eventually user-facing errors.

[00:55] Priya Kapoor: to add, we had an internal deploy earlier in the day, but we don't yet think it's causative; looks more like a traffic pattern combined with cache pressure. also, the fallback policy didn't go to the larger model variant, it fell back to a lower memory config and that increased CPU overhead.

[01:28] Jon Park: thanks. couple clarifying q's: when you say "kv cache evictions," is that uniform across all shards, or localized? and did you observe request routing switching regionally?

[01:45] Evan Morales: mostly localized to the hot-shards — about 60% of eviction events were on two pods handling the hot prefix. we did see some routing jitter, not full region failover, but a number of requests were retried and then routed to the fallback pool.

[02:12] Liam O'Connor: on the security side, we're looking at audit logs — some of the logs seem truncated; we need to make sure the retention and export configuration are capturing full traces. we also want confirmation about KMS usage for in-flight keys used for cache encryption.

[02:36] Maya Thompson: understood. Redwood will share the SOC2 docs and the audit-log export guide. Jon, can you walk through the metrics we pulled from our side — the KV miss/evict timeline and the fallback throughput?

[03:02] Jon Park: sure. attaching here, but quick callouts: evictions spiked at 02:17 and continued for ~28 minutes; KV hit rate dropped from 96% to about 58% in that window. fallback request ratio peaked at ~14% of total, and latency for fallback requests increased by ~2.5x compared to normal. our hypothesis: continuous batching + smaller KV working set caused excessive re-computation and memory thrash on the hot pods.

[03:45] Priya Kapoor: when you say "continuous batching" are you referring to runtime level batching or our request burst windows?

[03:58] Jon Park: runtime-level. Redwood's serving runtime does continuous batching to maximize GPU utilization; it maintains a KV cache per model shard. If many unique prefixes hit at once, the KV footprint grows and eviction policy kicks in. small working sets with high churn are worst.

[04:30] Evan Morales: one point that mattered: our tokens-per-request distribution shifted higher during the period because of a bot run from one of our customers. that increased KV allocations per request.

[04:52] Maya Thompson: ok — good to know. let's walk through immediate mitigations: rate limit the offending origin, increase KV cache size on the dedicated pool, and adjust fallback routing to prefer a slightly larger variant instead of the low-memory one. Jon, can you talk about feasibility?

[05:15] Jon Park: absolutely. we can do a quick config change to bump per-shard KV reserve by ~20% which will reduce evictions at the cost of memory headroom. we can also tweak routing so the fallback goes to a variant with more memory; downside is higher per-token cost. for a short pilot it's fine. autoscale thresholds can be relaxed to spin up more pods faster during similar spikes.

[05:50] Priya Kapoor: cost tradeoffs are ok for a 2-4 hour pilot; long term we'll want a more nuanced approach. are there heuristics for dynamic kv sizing?

[06:05] Jon Park: yes, there's an adaptive allocation we've been testing — it uses recent per-prefix footprint statistics to floor the KV allocation for hot prefixes. we'll simulate with your traffic and share results.

[06:26] Evan Morales: about the fallback behaviour — we had a canary rollback policy that should have flipped traffic to the larger pool, but due to an overlap with a rate-limiter policy it instead routed to a low-memory variant. seems like policy precedence was the problem.

[06:52] Nina Roy: that's an important callout — Redwood's policy engine evaluates routing rules in order, and sometimes deny/limit rules can take precedence. we can add a rule to ensure fallback to the larger variant when KB eviction rate exceeds X. we'll propose an ordered rule set.

[07:18] Liam O'Connor: on the auditing front, do you retain per-token IDs or user-identifiable metadata in the logs? we need guarantees about PII removal and redaction before logs leave the VPC.

[07:33] Maya Thompson: good question. Redwood's hosted mode redacts user content by default in the standard export. For Dedicated/Private we support customer-managed keying and also have options for redaction filters. I'll share the exact section in the security pack.

[07:58] Evan Morales: can you send that over? our compliance needs to see the exact retention windows and how to configure the export so nothing sensitive leaves our S3 bucket.

[08:09] Maya Thompson: yes — action item for me.

[08:15] Jon Park: back to mitigations — proposed short-term plan: 1) bump KV reserve on hot-shards, 2) adjust fallback route to medium variant, 3) temporarily loosen autoscale cooldowns, 4) rate-limit offending origin. We ran a tabletop earlier and expect that to reduce user errors while we run a sizing sim.

[08:44] Priya Kapoor: sounds good. what's the risk of increasing KV reserve? could this starve other tenants?

[08:58] Jon Park: for Dedicated pools, we can increase within the customer's pool without affecting others. For shared pools we'd be careful — but you're on a Dedicated pool correct?

[09:10] Evan Morales: yes Dedicated.

[09:15] Nina Roy: perfect — that simplifies things. Also we recommend a short canary: apply changes to 10% of traffic for 30m while monitoring latency and error rates. If good, roll to 100% over 1 hour.

[09:30] Evan Morales: ok how much ops effort for that canary?

[09:36] Jon Park: we can configure the canary via the console; SEs will coordinate the rollout and monitor. We'll need your confirmation window and a contact for on-call during the pilot.

[10:00] Priya Kapoor: we'll commit to a 3-hour window Thursday morning; Evan will be on-call.

[10:08] Maya Thompson: noted. next, some follow-up Qs from the Redwood risk team — Liam, you mentioned truncated logs; can you give an example?

[10:20] Liam O'Connor: we saw some span traces truncated at ~2KB; full trace IDs were missing in a few rows, making correlation hard. we want full trace retention for 30 days, then aggregated metrics beyond that. Is that feasible?

[10:35] Maya Thompson: yes. We'll share the export configuration. For Dedicated we can enable extended trace retention, but it may incur storage costs. We'll include estimates.

[10:47] Evan Morales: another quick question — the ticket mentioned a model variant mismatch; some requests were served by an older pinned version after fallback. How does rollout version pinning interact with fallback?

[11:05] Jon Park: rollouts are independent, but fallback policies select a compatible variant by architecture. If you pin version at route-level, fallback will only pick variants that satisfy the compatibility matrix. In your case, an older pinned route caused the fallback selector to choose a small-memory build. We should remove the hard pin for the route used by the pilot.

[11:32] Priya Kapoor: removing pin feels risky; can we do a canary that overrides pinning locally?

[11:42] Jon Park: yes — route-level override for canary is supported. we'll show the steps.

[11:55] Evan Morales: fine. we'll do an override during the pilot.

[12:03] Maya Thompson: let's walk through the runbook steps now — quick readout so everyone knows the sequence. Nina?

[12:10] Nina Roy: runbook: 1) Rate-limit offending origin at the edge (HarborGuard) — confirm done. 2) Redwood increments per-shard KV reserve by 20% on Dedicated pool (Jon). 3) Configure fallback policy to medium-variant and set policy precedence rule (Jon + Nina). 4) Start 10% canary for 30m — monitor latency, token errors, backend queue depth. 5) If metrics stable, expand to 50% for 30m, then 100%. 6) Collect full traces and attach to the incident ticket.

[12:56] Priya Kapoor: good. what monitoring dashboards should we watch?

[13:03] Jon Park: KV hit/miss, eviction rate, per-shard memory, request queue depth, fallback ratio, p99 latency, and error rate by route. We'll provide a pre-made dashboard link.

[13:20] Maya Thompson: I'll drop links after the call.

[13:26] Evan Morales: one more item — our legal wants an SLA addendum for higher availability during this pilot; is that a quick ask?

[13:36] Maya Thompson: for a short pilot we can provide a scoped commitment but a formal SLA addendum takes procurement. We can supply a written temporary commitment covering the pilot window.

[13:52] Liam O'Connor: and about encryption — KMS integration: do we support customer-controlled keys in Dedicated?

[14:00] Maya Thompson: yes; customer-managed KMS is available in Dedicated and in Private deployments. We'll share the integration guide.

[14:12] Priya Kapoor: thanks. any pros/cons to moving to Private for this workload?

[14:20] Jon Park: Private gives the tightest control — VPC-only egress, on-prem optional — but it's a lift and licensing. For now, Dedicated with customer KMS and extended retention should suffice.

[14:35] Priya Kapoor: ok we agree.

[14:40] Evan Morales: what about long-term mitigations — can Redwood help with adaptive KV sizing?

[14:47] Jon Park: yes — we'll run the sim against your traffic and propose a dynamic policy that floors allocations for hot prefixes. we can also add heuristics to pre-warm caches for known heavy prefixes.

[15:02] Priya Kapoor: pre-warm — interesting. is that manual or automated?

[15:08] Jon Park: both. you can declaratively list hot prefixes, or we can enable an automated detection that pre-warms based on recent access patterns. automated detection has a small false positive rate but helps with unknown bursts.

[15:28] Evan Morales: ok schedule-wise: when can Jon run the simulation?

[15:32] Jon Park: I can start with the dataset you provide as early as tomorrow, results in 3 days.

[15:40] Priya Kapoor: we'll get logs to you by Friday (2026-11-06).

[15:44] Maya Thompson: great - I'll recap action items in the follow-up email and attach the security pack and runbook. Anything else?

[15:52] Priya Kapoor: just a small ask — can you include cost estimates for running larger fallback variants during peak periods?

[15:58] Maya Thompson: yes, Jon will include per-hour delta for the pilot.

[16:05] Evan Morales: thanks all. we appreciate the quick help.

[16:12] Nina Roy: thanks team, we'll reconvene after the sim results.

[16:18] Maya Thompson: next meeting: pilot kickoff 2026-11-16 09:00 UTC — I'll send calendar invite after this.

[16:26] End of transcript.

Notes: transcript contains a few mis-heard words and timestamps are approximate; this is an auto-generated export and may omit short crosstalk lines.
